books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: William Graham Sumner, 'The Forgotten Man,' in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883)
Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
William Graham Sumner, “The Forgotten Man,” in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883):

“The type and formula of most schemes of philanthropy or humanitarianism is this: A and B put their heads together to decide what C shall be made to do for D. The radical vice of all these schemes, from a sociological point of view, is that C is not allowed a voice in the matter, and his position, character, and interests, as well as the ultimate effects on society through C’s interests, are entirely overlooked. I call C the Forgotten Man.”

Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889:

“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.”
stimulus.source_note: William Graham Sumner, 'The Forgotten Man,' in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883); Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889. Both quotations are exact.

stem: Which claim would both Sumner and Carnegie most likely accept?

options.text: Government should own the railroads and all the telegraphs
options.misconception: Neither man asks government to own industry; Sumner opposes government schemes.

options.text: All wealth should be divided equally among all citizens
options.misconception: Neither man favors equal division; Carnegie praises the rich administering wealth.

options.text: Great fortunes are natural, not a wrong for government to correct
The state should guarantee a job to every single worker
options.misconception: Neither man asks the state to guarantee jobs; Sumner rejects state aid schemes.

rationales.A: Neither man asks government to own industry; Sumner opposes government schemes.
rationales.B: Neither man favors equal division; Carnegie praises the rich administering wealth.
rationales.C: Background from the books: both men treat great wealth as the fruit of progress, not a wrong to fix.
rationales.D: Neither man asks the state to guarantee jobs; Sumner rejects state aid schemes.
rationales.general:
Find the ground both men share.
1. Sumner treats success as the reward of fitness, not a wrong to undo.
2. Background from the books: Carnegie calls the rise of great fortunes a change to welcome.
3. Both men defend the rich against the charge that wealth itself is unjust.
4. They part on what the rich should do, but neither asks government to correct fortunes.
Remember: two writers can share a premise and still reach different duties.
